caption:
Heating on? Keep the room your baby sleeps in at 16 to 20°C (about 61 to 68°F).

WHY: the NHS says overheating can increase the risk of SIDS (sudden infant death syndrome). The Lullaby Trust recommends 16 to 20°C so babies don't get too hot.

HOW (Lullaby Trust, NHS):
1. Put a room thermometer in the room where your baby sleeps. It's hard to guess the temperature.
2. Use a well-fitting baby sleeping bag, or lightweight bedding firmly tucked in no higher than their shoulders. No loose blankets, duvets or pillows in the cot.
3. Baby's skin hot or sweaty? Take off one or more layers.
4. Take hats and extra clothing off as soon as you come indoors. Babies don't need hats indoors.

THE CATCH: hands and feet usually feel cooler, and that's normal. Feel their chest or the back of their neck instead.

Do this: tonight, put a room thermometer in the room where your baby sleeps.

Send this to whoever puts your baby down at their place.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#safesleep #newborn #newparents #babysleep #sids
first_comment: Sources (checked Nov 4 2026; re-checked Nov 5 2026): The Lullaby Trust, 'What is the ideal baby room temperature?' (https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/safer-sleep-advice/baby-room-temperature/, last reviewed 1 February 2025, updated April 30 2026): "The recommended room temperature for babies is 16-20°C so that they don't get too hot."; "use a room thermometer in the rooms where your baby sleeps"; "feel your baby's chest or the back of their neck (your baby's hands and feet will usually be cooler, which is normal)"; "Babies do not need to wear hats indoors."; "If your baby's skin is hot or sweaty, remove one or more layers of bedclothes or bedding." NHS, 'Reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)' (https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/reduce-the-risk-of-sudden-infant-death-syndrome/, last reviewed 25 November 2025): "keep the room at a temperature between about 16 to 20C – monitor the temperature using a room thermometer"; "Overheating can increase the risk of SIDS."; "remove hats and extra clothing as soon as you come indoors"; remove 1 or more layers of clothing or bedding if your baby's skin is hot or sweating; "use lightweight blankets, sheets or a baby sleeping bag". °F values are maths (16°C = 60.8°F, 20°C = 68°F). The Lullaby Trust, 'Keeping a clear cot' (https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/baby-safety/safer-sleep-information/keeping-a-clear-cot/, last reviewed 1 February 2025): "all the baby needs is lightweight bedding, firmly tucked in no higher than their shoulders, or a baby sleeping bag."; "The bedding should be appropriate to the room temperature, firmly tucked in and not soft or bulky." NHS (same SIDS page): "do not use pillows, duvets, cot bumpers, loose blankets, soft toys or anything to keep your baby in place".
alt_text: Littlefold Reel, drawn sunny sky. A wall thermometer on the wall beside a crib with a drawn baby asleep on their back in a pink sleep bag. The red line sits in a sage band between 16 and 20 and settles at 18; a berry tag '16–20°C' and 'just right ✓'. Close-up of the crib: little sweat drops by the baby's head, 'hot or sweaty?', then a small blue baby top floats up and away, 'one layer off' and a check. No blanket in the crib. A knit hat with a 'no' ring floats off the baby's head, 'hat off' and a check. Do this: the thermometer pops onto the wall beside the crib reading 18, a '18°C' tag beside the reading, a check and hearts. On screen: heating on? Baby's room: 16 to 20°C. About 61 to 68°F. Check them: too warm? Take a layer off. Hot or sweaty? Take off some clothes. And: indoors, babies don't need a hat. Take it off when you get home. Do this: Put a room thermometer in their room. Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.
